timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults on the general surgical wards who are able to take oral medicines receive paracetamol orally rather than intravenously on the day after surgery?
why: IV paracetamol is costly and is often continued after patients start eating and drinking. No audit of IV-to-oral paracetamol after surgery exists in the library.

standard.wording: Do not offer intravenous paracetamol unless the person cannot take oral medicine.

population: Adults on general surgical wards on postoperative day 1 who are documented as tolerating oral fluids. Exclude patients nil by mouth for a stated clinical reason.
sample: 40 consecutive postoperative patients over 2 weeks (point prevalence on ward rounds is acceptable).
data_source: EPMA administration records; nursing fluid charts; ward round notes for oral intake status.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Change the postoperative EPMA order set so oral paracetamol is the default and IV paracetamol needs a reason with a 24-hour auto-stop.
reaudit: Next 40 postoperative patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical audit meeting and drugs and therapeutics committee. If it works, keep the order set and share the cost saving.
evidence: [3030] IV metronidazole despite oral suitability 81.4% → 34.2% after education
[2208] Oral metronidazole use 12.5% → 61% in an acute surgical unit
[1517] Electronic prescribing order set: analgesia protocol compliance 0% → 58%
pitfalls: Oral intake status is poorly recorded → use the fluid chart and ward round note together.
Anaesthetists prescribe IV paracetamol in recovery → involve them in the order set change.
Nausea is used as a blanket reason → accept only documented vomiting.
Gains fade after the pharmacist leaves → rely on the order set, not reminders.
pearls: Recruit the surgical ward pharmacist.
Show the cost difference per day.
Collect data on two ward rounds a week for speed.
Pair with oral ibuprofen for a single analgesia message.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from EPMA
pass: On postoperative day 1, every paracetamol dose given is oral (or rectal) in a patient documented as able to take oral fluids or medicines.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults after elective abdominal or hernia surgery are prescribed regular oral ibuprofen for the first 24 hours unless contraindicated?
why: Multimodal analgesia reduces opioid use, yet NSAIDs are often left off without a reason. Postoperative analgesia audits in the library are mainly orthopaedic [1517][1321]; none has audited NSAID prescribing after general surgery against NG180.

standard.wording: Offer oral ibuprofen to manage immediate postoperative pain of all severities (including pain after dental surgery) unless the person has had surgery for hip fracture (see the recommendations on analgesia in the NICE guideline on hip fracture).

population: Adults having elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, hernia repair or other elective abdominal surgery. Exclude hip fracture surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive elective cases over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Theatre system for the case list; EPMA for postoperative prescriptions; pre-operative assessment notes for contraindications.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add regular oral ibuprofen to the elective general surgery postoperative order set, with a contraindication checklist that removes it when ticked.
reaudit: Next 40 elective cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the surgical and anaesthetic audit meeting. If it works, keep the order set and report opioid use as a balancing measure.
evidence: [1517] Enhanced recovery order set: compliance 0% → 58%, ibuprofen 58%
[1321] Arthroplasty analgesia: protocol standard 34% → 61%, 87% of adherent cases used the powerplan
[2020] Analgesic ladder compliance 83.3% → 50.9% after teaching only
pitfalls: Surgeons worry about anastomotic leak → agree colorectal exceptions before cycle 1.
Renal function is not checked → build eGFR into the checklist.
Day-case patients are prescribed on discharge only → count TTO prescriptions too.
Opioid use goes up if NSAIDs are missed → record opioid doses as a balance.
pearls: Recruit a pain team nurse.
Use EPMA reports to pull data quickly.
Start with day-case lists, where the change is least contested.
Report AKI rates to reassure colleagues.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA
pass: Regular oral ibuprofen (or another oral NSAID) is prescribed for the first 24 hours after surgery, or a contraindication is documented (for example AKI, eGFR <30, active GI bleeding, NSAID allergy, surgeon request after anastomosis).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults referred on the suspected lower GI cancer pathway (excluding rectal or anal mass or anal ulceration) have a FIT result available at triage?
why: FIT at ≥10 µg Hb/g is now the gateway to the colorectal suspected cancer pathway. One unit went from 7 of 74 to 18 of 18 FIT use [2080]; a large trust found 103 cancers referred without FIT [2753]. No closed loop against the 2023 NICE wording is in the library.

standard.wording: 1.3.1 ... People with a rectal mass, an unexplained anal mass or unexplained anal ulceration do not need to be offered FIT before referral is considered. [2023] 1.3.2 Refer adults using a suspected cancer pathway referral for colorectal cancer if they have a FIT result of at least 10 micrograms of haemoglobin per gram of faeces. [2023]

population: Adults referred on the lower GI suspected cancer pathway. Exclude referrals for rectal mass, anal mass or anal ulceration.
sample: 50 consecutive referrals over the last 4 weeks.
data_source: Cancer referral booking system; referral forms; pathology system for FIT result and date; triage notes.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Make a FIT result a required field on the electronic lower GI referral form, with referral returned to the GP with a FIT kit if blank (safety-netted for strong clinical concern).
reaudit: Next 50 referrals 3 months after the form change, same template.
close_loop: Present to the cancer alliance and colorectal MDT. If it works, keep the form rule and monitor monthly with the cancer services manager.
evidence: [2080] qFIT in 2WW referrals: 7/74 eligible → 18/18 after a closed loop
[2753] FIT-negative referrals: 103 of 1,037 cancers had no FIT
[3534] Memory clinic referral proforma: all blood tests 11.9% → 80% when proforma used
pitfalls: GPs object to returned referrals → agree the rule and safety-net with the primary care lead first.
FIT done after referral is counted as a pass → use 'available at triage' as the fixed time.
Patients who cannot return a sample are penalised → allow a documented exception.
Local form versions vary → check the form in use in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the colorectal cancer pathway navigator.
Pull data weekly from the referral system.
Report conversion rates by FIT band to show value.
Share results with the cancer alliance, which may fund changes.
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from referral and pathology systems
pass: A quantitative FIT result is on the referral or in the pathology system at the time of straight-to-test triage.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults needing immediate emergency laparotomy have their pre-operative CT reported by a senior radiologist within one hour of the scan?
why: Delayed CT reports slow the path to theatre in peritonitis and ischaemia. Library audits cover time to CT [2588][2841] and CT discrepancies [2682], but none has audited report time and grade against the NELA standard.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), CT scanning and reporting, citing RCS The High-Risk General Surgical Patient 2018
standard.wording: For patients requiring immediate surgery CT scanning should be undertaken immediately. CT results should be reported by a senior radiologist (ST3 and above) within one hour of being undertaken, regardless of urgency of request.

population: Adults in NELA who had immediate surgery (RCS definitions: peritonitis, perforation, ischaemia, haemorrhage, strangulation, tender obstruction or sepsis) and a pre-operative CT.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible NELA cases over the last 6 months.
data_source: NELA data extract (Q2.7 CT time, report time, reporter grade); RIS for scan and report timestamps; outsourced reporting logs.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: A 'NELA urgent' flag on the CT request that sends the scan to the top of the reporting worklist and prompts a phone call to the surgical registrar.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint surgical–radiology meeting and NELA local governance. If it works, keep the flag and review monthly with the NELA lead.
evidence: [2588] NELA QI: time to CT 2 d 19 h → <4 h, 30-day mortality 11.1% → 2.4%
[2682] Emergency laparotomy CT discrepancy 27.2% → 5.8%; only 23% reported within 24 h in cycle 1
[2656] Acute abdomen pathway: imaging within timeframe 60% → 78%
pitfalls: NELA fields are incomplete → cross-check times on RIS.
Outsourced reports lack reporter grade → ask the provider for grade data.
Radiology feels blamed → co-present with a radiology trainee.
Night-time cases dominate breaches → report by time of day.
pearls: Recruit the NELA lead and a radiology registrar.
Use the NELA extract to find cases in minutes.
Include surgeon–radiologist discussion as a second measure.
Show time from report to theatre alongside.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from NELA extract and RIS
pass: CT report (preliminary or final) issued by a radiologist ST3 or above within 60 minutes of scan completion.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults having emergency laparotomy with suspected sepsis receive antibiotics within one hour of the first qualifying NEWS2 score?
why: Delayed antibiotics in surgical sepsis raise mortality. One pathway audit fell from 80% to 50% in septic patients despite changes [2656]. No closed-loop audit against the NELA 2025 antibiotic standard is in the library.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), infection management, citing AoMRC 2022 and RCS HRGSP 2018
standard.wording: Patients with a suspected “surgical” source of infection and NEWS2 of 5+, or >=3 in any one variable, should receive antimicrobials within 1 hour of recorded NEWS2 abnormality.

population: Adults in NELA with suspected sepsis at arrival or at decision to operate. Patients with NEWS2 1–4 are recorded separately against the 3-hour standard.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible NELA cases over the last 6 months.
data_source: NELA extract (Q2.10, Q2.11); ED observations system for NEWS2 times; EPMA or ED drug chart for administration time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: A 'surgical sepsis' PGD allowing ED and SAU nurses to give first-dose antibiotics from the trust guideline once NEWS2 ≥5 with suspected abdominal source.
reaudit: Next 40 eligible NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at the NELA governance meeting and to ED/SAU nursing leads. If it works, keep the PGD and report monthly via NELA.
evidence: [2656] Acute abdomen pathway: antibiotics within 1 h for septic patients 80% → 50%
[1200] Open fracture antibiotics: mean time 271 → 233 min, STAT prescriptions 15.4% → 51.7%
[1328] Necrotising fasciitis: all confirmed cases had sepsis six within 1 h
pitfalls: Prescription time is used instead of administration time → use administration only.
NEWS2 is recorded late → use the first observations timestamp.
ED and surgery each think the other owns antibiotics → agree ownership in the pathway.
PGD approval takes time → start with a pre-printed stat prescription.
pearls: Recruit an ED sepsis nurse.
Record where the patient was at the trigger point.
Present individual delayed cases anonymously.
Use NELA data so cycle 2 needs no extra collection.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from NELA and ED records
pass: First antibiotic dose administered within 60 minutes of the first recorded NEWS2 ≥5 (or a single parameter scoring 3).
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults having emergency laparotomy have a mortality risk score documented at the end of surgery?
why: The end-of-operation risk decides critical care admission, yet audits in the library measure only the pre-operative score [2403][2547][2038]. No audit of the postoperative risk reassessment is in the library.

standard.source: NELA Principal Standards (February 2025), risk assessment, citing RCS HRGSP 2018 p37
standard.wording: Patients should have their risk of in-hospital mortality reassessed and documented at the end of surgery, using risk prediction tools and clinical judgement. Patients with an end-of-operation risk of death of 5%+, by any measure, should be admitted directly to critical care.

population: Adults (≥18) included in NELA.
sample: 40 consecutive NELA cases over the last 3 months.
data_source: NELA extract (Q6.1 postoperative risk); operation note; anaesthetic chart; critical care admission log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: Add a mandatory 'End-of-surgery NELA risk: __%' field to the emergency laparotomy operation note template, completed at sign-out.
reaudit: Next 40 NELA cases, same template.
close_loop: Present at NELA governance and the emergency theatre meeting. If it works, keep the op note field and link it to the critical care referral.
evidence: [2517] NELA frailty: CFS recorded 0% → 92% after a proforma item
[2403] NELA score on CEPOD forms in about 21%; missing in up to 97% of files
[2529] High-risk patients admitted directly to critical care: 38 of 43
pitfalls: The score is entered in NELA later but not in notes → count only contemporaneous documentation.
Surgeons and anaesthetists each expect the other to do it → name the anaesthetist at sign-out.
Intraoperative data are missing → allow a documented clinical estimate.
Template fields become default values → spot-check against NELA calculations.
pearls: Recruit the NELA anaesthetic lead.
Add the NELA calculator link to the op note.
Report the proportion of ≥5% cases reaching critical care alongside.
Build it into the WHO sign-out question.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from NELA and notes
pass: A numerical mortality risk (NELA, P-POSSUM or similar) is written on the operation note, anaesthetic record or immediate postoperative plan.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults with bowel perforation or ischaemia managed without surgery who die in hospital receive direct input from the palliative care team?
why: NELA now audits patients who do not have a laparotomy (NoLap), and many of them die in hospital. No audit of palliative care input after a non-operative decision is in the library.

standard.source: NELA NoLap Standards of Care (from April 2024), end-of-life care, citing RCS Caring for Patients Nearing the End of Life
standard.wording: The surgeon should seek to discuss the patient’s case with relevant professionals to ascertain: • the appropriate treatment options at the end of life available to the patient • the patients’ wishes, preferences and beliefs to inform their best interests. A formal consultation with the palliative care team is particularly useful in this context.

population: Adults (≥18) with bowel perforation or ischaemia where surgery was indicated but not done, who died in hospital.
sample: All eligible cases over the last 12 months (expect 20–40 in a DGH).
data_source: NELA NoLap extract or ICD-10 case list; notes; palliative care team referral log; individualised end-of-life care plan.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

change: An automatic palliative care referral prompt in the NoLap proforma when the consultant records a non-operative decision.
reaudit: All eligible cases over the 6 months after the change, same template.
close_loop: Present at emergency surgery mortality and morbidity meeting and to the palliative care team. If it works, keep the prompt and report through NELA NoLap.
evidence: [1915] Hospital deaths with dementia: palliative care involved in 40%
[1849] Advance care planning: treatment escalation plan 41% → 75% after an intervention
[1784] NACEL round two: individualised end-of-life plan in 71% of deaths
pitfalls: Patients die within hours, before referral is possible → record time from decision to death and analyse short survivors separately.
Palliative teams are small out of hours → accept telephone advice documented in notes.
Case finding misses non-operated patients → use the NoLap ICD-10 algorithm and M&M lists.
Surgeons feel judged about the decision → keep the audit on care, not the decision.
pearls: Recruit a palliative care consultant as co-lead.
Use the NELA NoLap extract for case finding.
Include the end-of-life care plan as a second measure.
Share anonymised family feedback if available.
effort: ~25 min per 10 patients from notes
pass: A palliative care team member reviewed the patient in person (or by documented direct consultation) before death.
timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit

question: What proportion of adults with a CT-confirmed ureteric stone and ongoing pain, or a stone unlikely to pass, have surgical treatment (ureteroscopy or lithotripsy) within 48 hours of diagnosis?
why: Early definitive treatment reduces stents, repeat procedures and readmissions. Renal colic audits mostly measure CT timing and analgesia; only two report time to definitive treatment [2600][2471], and emergency stenting often replaces treatment.

standard.wording: Offer surgical treatment (including SWL) to adults with ureteric stones and renal colic within 48 hours of diagnosis or readmission, if: pain is ongoing and not tolerated or the stone is unlikely to pass.

pass: Ureteroscopy or shockwave lithotripsy started within 48 hours of the diagnostic CT (or of readmission). A stent or nephrostomy alone does not count, except in obstructed infected kidneys, which are excluded.
population: Adults (≥18) with a ureteric stone on CT KUB who meet either NG118 criterion (ongoing pain not tolerated, or stone unlikely to pass, e.g. ≥10 mm or failed trial). Exclude obstructed infected kidney needing urgent decompression, pregnancy, solitary renal stones and patients who decline surgery.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible adults over the last 3 months (extend to 6 months in low-volume units).
data_source: Radiology system for CT date/time and stone size; urology admission list and EPR for indication; theatre and lithotripsy systems for procedure date/time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
If yes, clock starts at readmission

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Ring-fence a daily 'hot stone' slot (ureteroscopy list or lithotripsy session) that the urology registrar books directly from the morning trauma/take meeting.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible adults, same template and same clock start.
close_loop: Present at urology governance and to theatre management with the stent and readmission counts. If it works, make the hot slot permanent in the theatre template and report the 48-hour rate monthly.
evidence: [2600] acute ureteric stones: treatment within 48 hours 35% → 53% (hot primary ureteroscopy theatre)
[2471] renal colic benchmark: surgical intervention within 48 hours 70% → 100% (renal order-set and leaflet)
[2026] ureteric colic: teaching only; clinic within 4 weeks only 26.4% after the change (teaching alone fails)
pitfalls: Clock start is disputed (ED arrival, CT, urology review) → fix it as CT report time and keep it the same in both cycles.
Cases miscounted when a stent is the only procedure → record the first procedure separately and count stents as fails unless infection is present.
Small numbers per month in small units → extend the look-back rather than shortening the window.
Theatre managers resist ring-fenced time → show stent change episodes and readmissions avoided, not just the percentage.
Gains fade when the rota changes → put the hot slot in the theatre template, not in a consultant's goodwill.
pearls: Recruit the stone lead and the theatre manager before cycle 1.
Agree 'unlikely to pass' (e.g. ≥10 mm or failed 4-week trial) before collecting.
Log delay reasons; they show which resource to ask for.
Pair with the stent database to show downstream stent burden.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from radiology, EPR and theatre systems

question: What proportion of men catheterised for acute urinary retention are prescribed an alpha blocker before their trial without catheter?
why: Alpha blockers before catheter removal raise the chance of voiding successfully. One ED audit found tamsulosin started in only 36% of men with retention [2257]; no closed-loop audit of this step has been published in the library.

standard.wording: Offer an alpha blocker to men for managing acute urinary retention before removal of the catheter. [2010]

pass: Alpha blocker (e.g. tamsulosin 400 micrograms) prescribed from the day of catheterisation or before the trial without catheter, on the drug chart, discharge prescription or GP letter; or a contraindication documented. Men already taking an alpha blocker pass if it is continued.
population: Men (≥18) catheterised for first-episode acute urinary retention in ED or on the urology take. Exclude clot retention, postoperative retention, known neurogenic bladder and men listed directly for prostate surgery without a trial.
sample: 40 consecutive men over the last 3 months.
data_source: ED and urology EPR for catheterisation date; e-prescribing or drug chart and discharge letter for the alpha blocker; trial-without-catheter clinic list for the TWOC date.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an 'acute urinary retention' order set in ED and urology e-prescribing that includes tamsulosin 400 micrograms once daily and books the trial without catheter.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 consecutive men, same template.
close_loop: Present at the joint ED–urology meeting. If it works, keep the order set, add it to the ED retention pathway and include TWOC success rate in the urology dashboard.
evidence: [2257] ED acute retention pathway: tamsulosin started in 36%, DRE 18% (baseline, no re-audit)
[2514] day-case surgery: pre-populated discharge order set, correct medicines 25% → 83%
[2471] renal colic: order-set raised NSAID use 54.5% → 71.9%
pitfalls: ED doctors discharge before prescribing → put the order set in ED, not only on the ward.
Alpha blocker recorded only in the GP letter → accept the discharge prescription as evidence and check both.
Mixing postoperative retention into the sample lowers the rate → apply the exclusions from the start.
Clinic TWOC outcomes missing → record TWOC outcome but do not make it a pass criterion.
Order set ignored after rotation → make it the default pathway item and brief new ED starters.
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and the urology nurse specialist who runs the TWOC clinic.
Pull cases from the TWOC clinic list; it captures most retention episodes.
Show TWOC success by alpha blocker status; it persuades sceptics.
Agree the dose and the start day before cycle 1.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from EPR and e-prescribing

question: What proportion of patients whose first TURBT shows high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer have a second TURBT within 6 weeks?
why: Re-resection finds residual and upstaged tumour in high-risk disease. TURBT quality has been audited [3037][2763], but no audit in the library measures whether and when the re-resection happens.

standard.wording: If the first TURBT shows high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, offer another TURBT as soon as possible and no later than 6 weeks after the first resection.

pass: Second TURBT performed ≤42 days after the first TURBT.
population: Adults with a first TURBT showing high-risk NMIBC (high grade/G3 pTa or pT1, with or without CIS). Exclude muscle-invasive disease, patients going straight to radical cystectomy, and patients who decline or are unfit (record these separately).
sample: All eligible patients over the last 12 months (expect 30–50 in a DGH).
data_source: Urology cancer MDT database and pathology for case list and risk group; theatre system for both TURBT dates; cancer tracker for delays.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make the MDT outcome for high-risk NMIBC automatically list the re-TURBT with a 'must be done by' date (day 42) on the waiting list, tracked by the cancer tracker.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: all new high-risk NMIBC since the change (at least 3 months), same template.
close_loop: Present at the urology cancer MDT and cancer governance. If it works, keep the MDT listing rule and add the re-TURBT interval to the bladder cancer dashboard.
evidence: [2029] mitomycin after TURBT: theatre–pharmacy system change cut delay 7.66 → 4.24 hours
[3033] open surgeon-level reporting improved TURBT resection quality
[3037] detrusor muscle sampling 39% → 66% (separate base specimen pot and dedicated surgeons)

Report median days and the 42-day rate together.
Link to theatre scheduling so re-TURBTs get protected slots.
Include residual tumour and upstaging rates to show why it matters.
effort: ~30 min per 10 patients from MDT database and theatre system

question: What proportion of men starting androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer are offered a supervised exercise programme?
why: Supervised resistance and aerobic exercise reduces fatigue and improves quality of life on ADT. Bone health on ADT has been audited [1349], but no audit in the library measures the exercise offer.

standard.source: NICE NG131 rec 1.4.19 (2019, updated 2021; rec from 2014)
standard.wording: Offer people who are starting or having androgen deprivation therapy supervised resistance and aerobic exercise at least twice a week for 12 weeks to reduce fatigue and improve quality of life. [2014]

pass: Clinic letter or nurse specialist record documents an offer of, or referral to, a supervised exercise programme within 3 months of the first ADT dose.
population: Men starting ADT (LHRH agonist/antagonist or orchidectomy) for prostate cancer. Exclude men on end-of-life care and men already in a supervised exercise programme.
sample: 40 consecutive men who started ADT in the last 6 months.
data_source: Uro-oncology clinic letters and CNS records; ADT start date from the prescribing record or first-injection record; exercise service referral log.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'Supervised exercise programme offered: accepted / declined' line to the ADT start clinic template with a one-click referral to the local programme.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 men starting ADT, same template.
close_loop: Present at the urology cancer MDT and the cancer alliance living-with-cancer group. If it works, keep the template line and report uptake yearly.

question: What proportion of women seen for the first time in a continence clinic with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder have a completed bladder diary of at least 3 days?
why: A bladder diary guides diagnosis and treatment choice, and avoids repeat visits. LUTS pathway audits show large gaps after referral [2797]; no audit in the library measures bladder diary use.

standard.wording: Use bladder diaries in the initial assessment of women with urinary incontinence or overactive bladder. Encourage women to complete a minimum of 3 days of the diary covering variations in their usual activities, such as both working and leisure days. [2006]

pass: A bladder diary covering ≥3 days is recorded or scanned in the notes by the end of the first specialist appointment.
population: Women (≥18) at a first urology, urogynaecology or continence clinic appointment for urinary incontinence or OAB. Exclude catheterised women and follow-up appointments.
sample: 40 consecutive new women over the last 2 months.
data_source: Clinic letters and scanned notes; appointment system for the case list.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Have the booking system send a 3-day bladder diary with every new continence appointment letter, with instructions to bring it.
reaudit: Wk 13–14: next 40 new women, same template.
close_loop: Present at the pelvic floor MDT. If it works, keep the automatic insert and measure repeat-visit rates.
evidence: [2797] benign LUTS after negative cancer referral: 59% had no documented advice, pathway or follow-up
[2643] post-tonsillectomy discharge: one-click inserts raised key advice 21% → 93%
[2004] TCI form change removed listing errors (6 → 0)

Booking team cannot add inserts → ask for an electronic letter template change or a text link.
Different clinics use different diaries → agree one 3-day format.

Record whether a diary was sent; it separates system failure from patient factors.

question: What proportion of discharges from critical care to a general ward between 22:00 and 07:00 are reported as adverse incidents?

standard.wording: After the decision to transfer a patient from a critical care area to the general ward has been made, he or she should be transferred as early as possible during the day. Transfer from critical care areas to the general ward between 10:00pm and 7:00am should be avoided whenever possible, and should be documented as an adverse incident if it occurs.

pass: A ward transfer between 22:00 and 07:00 has a matching incident report (Datix or equivalent).
population: All adult discharges from ICU/HDU to a general ward. Exclude transfers to another critical care unit, theatre, or deaths.

Decision time and actual time confused → record both; the standard is about actual transfer.
Small numbers → use all discharges over 3 months, not a sample.
Bed managers push back → invite them to the presentation and show readmission data.

question: In adults admitted to critical care from a ward or the emergency department, what proportion have a documented admission decision involving both the referring consultant and the critical care consultant?
why: Consultant-to-consultant discussion improves decisions about escalation, but library ICU audits look at NEWS2 before admission [507] and frailty scoring [2766], not who made the admission decision.

standard.wording: If the team caring for the patient considers that admission to a critical care area is clinically indicated, then the decision to admit should involve both the consultant caring for the patient on the ward and the consultant in critical care.

pass: The ICU admission note or referral record names both the parent-team consultant and the critical care consultant as involved in the decision.
population: Unplanned adult admissions to ICU/HDU from wards or ED. Exclude planned post-operative admissions, direct theatre admissions and cardiac arrest admissions.
sample: 40 consecutive unplanned admissions over the last 2 months.
data_source: ICU admission clerking and referral proforma; parent-team notes; ICU admissions log.

Definitions drift → lock the exclusion list before cycle 1.

question: In adults in critical care at risk of long-term problems, what proportion have rehabilitation goals agreed and documented within 4 days of admission or before critical care discharge, whichever is sooner?
why: NCEPOD's 2025 report 'Recovery beyond survival' found comprehensive rehabilitation assessments often missing. No closed-loop audit of rehabilitation goals after critical illness is in the library; the closest shows structured documentation doubled goal setting in a rehabilitation unit [1804].

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 1 (2017), from NICE CG83 rec 1.4
standard.wording: Adults in critical care at risk of morbidity have their rehabilitation goals agreed within 4 days of admission to critical care or before discharge from critical care, whichever is sooner.

pass: Short-term and medium-term rehabilitation goals documented (by any member of the critical care MDT) by day 4 of admission, or before discharge if the stay was shorter.
population: Adults admitted to ICU/HDU who meet any 'at risk' criterion on a short clinical assessment (e.g. ventilated, stay expected >4 days, unable to get out of bed independently, premorbid mobility problems). Exclude deaths and end-of-life care within 4 days.
sample: 40 consecutive at-risk admissions over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ICU notes and physiotherapy/OT records (rehabilitation goals, dates); ICU admission system (admission and discharge dates).

reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive at-risk admissions, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU MDT governance. If it works, add the goals to the ICU discharge summary so they travel to the ward.

At-risk definition changes between cycles → write the criteria on the data sheet.
Weekend admissions missed → report weekday and weekend admissions separately.

Use the NCEPOD 2025 audit toolkit fields where they match.
Present with a patient story from the follow-up clinic.
Add the box to the day-3 ward round so it is part of routine care.

question: In adults at risk of long-term problems who move from critical care to a general ward, what proportion have a written handover that includes their rehabilitation programme?
why: ICU discharge letters were poor in a UHBW audit [77] and handover information was often incomplete at the theatre–critical care interface [2247]; no audit in the library checks that rehabilitation plans reach the ward.

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 2 (2017), from NICE CG83 rec 1.12 and CG50 rec 1.15
standard.wording: Adults at risk of morbidity have a formal handover of care, including their agreed individualised structured rehabilitation programme, when they transfer from critical care to a general ward.

pass: The ICU discharge summary or handover document contains the rehabilitation goals and the plan (therapy frequency, mobility level, referrals) for the ward team.
population: Adults discharged alive from ICU/HDU to a general ward who met an 'at risk' criterion during the stay. Exclude transfers to other hospitals and palliative discharges.

question: In adults who stayed in critical care for more than 4 days and were at risk of long-term problems, what proportion are reviewed 2 to 3 months after critical care discharge?
why: NCEPOD's 2025 report 'Recovery beyond survival' found a lack of follow-up after intensive care. No audit of post-ICU follow-up is in the library.

standard.source: NICE QS158 statement 4 (2017), from NICE CG83 recs 1.1 and 1.23
standard.wording: Adults who stayed in critical care for more than 4 days and were at risk of morbidity have a review 2 to 3 months after discharge from critical care.

question: In adults who had a critical care stay and received rehabilitation on the ward, what proportion are given their own copy of the critical care discharge summary before leaving hospital?

question: At pre-operative assessment, what proportion of adults aged over 80 or with diabetes have a lying-to-standing or sitting-to-standing blood pressure recorded?
why: Postural hypotension raises the risk of postoperative falls and longer stay. The 2026 guideline added postural screening; no library audit has measured it, and intra-operative hypotension audits show the gap [1912].

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026), recommendation 6
standard.wording: Patients at risk of postural hypotension including those who are symptomatic, aged > 80 y or who are diabetic, should be screened with a supine-to-stand blood pressure assessment or a sit-to-stand assessment (if more pragmatic).

pass: A lying (or sitting) and standing blood pressure pair documented at the pre-assessment visit, with action recorded if the drop is ≥20/10 mmHg.
population: Adults aged over 80, or with diabetes, or with postural symptoms, attending nurse-led or anaesthetist pre-assessment for elective surgery. Exclude patients who cannot stand.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible pre-assessment attendances over 2 weeks.
data_source: Pre-assessment record (observations, history); electronic pre-op assessment system.

Telephone pre-assessments cannot measure it → exclude them and report the proportion.
Drops found but not acted on → add a 'drop found: action' field.

Report the number of significant drops found; it motivates staff.
Use the same eligibility list in both cycles.

question: Of elective operations cancelled on the day for high blood pressure, what proportion had a blood pressure below 180/120 mmHg?
why: Day-of-surgery cancellations waste theatre time; the 2026 guideline states surgery should proceed below stage 3 hypertension. Library cancellation audits focus on fasting and fitness [2170] [2724], not blood pressure thresholds.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists and British and Irish Hypertension Society, Measurement and management of adult blood pressure in the peri-operative period (Anaesthesia 2026)
standard.wording: A blood pressure measurement should be performed in the pre-operative clinic using best practice as outlined in this guideline. Surgery should proceed unless the blood pressure is ≥ 180/120 (stage 3 hypertension).

population: Adult elective cases cancelled on the day of surgery with blood pressure recorded as a reason. Exclude cardiac, obstetric and endocrine surgery (outside the guideline scope).
sample: All such cancellations over the last 12 months (expect 20–50 in a DGH).
data_source: Theatre cancellation log (reason codes); day-of-surgery observations; anaesthetic pre-op note.

question: In adults having general anaesthesia with at least one PONV risk factor, what proportion receive prophylaxis with two antiemetic interventions?
why: Nausea and vomiting after surgery delays discharge and is one of the most disliked outcomes. The library has only incidental PONV data within ERAS audits [2864]; no closed-loop audit of risk-based prophylaxis exists.

standard.source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 3
standard.wording: Guideline 3. Administer PONV prophylaxis using 2 interventions in adults at any risk for PONV ... Since most adult patients undergoing surgery and anesthesia will have at least one risk factor for PONV, a general multimodal approach is recommended for administering PONV prophylaxis.

pass: Two prophylactic interventions from different classes (e.g. dexamethasone plus ondansetron, or one drug plus TIVA) recorded on the anaesthetic chart.
population: Adults (18+) having general anaesthesia for elective or emergency surgery with ≥1 Apfel risk factor (female, non-smoker, history of PONV or motion sickness, postoperative opioids). Exclude patients going to ICU ventilated.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible cases from mixed day-case and inpatient lists over 2 weeks.
data_source: Electronic anaesthetic chart (antiemetics, TIVA); pre-op assessment (risk factors); recovery chart (PONV, rescue).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a default 'PONV prophylaxis: dexamethasone + ondansetron (untick with reason)' bundle to the electronic anaesthetic chart.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: 40 consecutive eligible cases, same lists and template.
close_loop: Present at the anaesthetic department meeting with recovery PONV rates. If it works, keep the chart bundle and add PONV to the recovery quality dashboard.
evidence: [2864] Elective colorectal ERAS audit: >90% compliance with PONV prophylaxis within an ERAS pathway (single cycle)
[1341] Queen Elizabeth Birmingham surgery: antiemetic co-prescribing with opioids >75% after education and reminders
[1421] Italian orthopaedic theatres without PACU: 6 of 261 patients failed discharge criteria for nausea/vomiting (single cycle)
pitfalls: Dexamethasone avoided in diabetes → record the reason; a documented alternative counts.
Apfel score not documented → derive it from the notes and keep the same method in both cycles.
Anaesthetists resist 'recipe' anaesthesia → keep an untick-with-reason option.
PONV outcome under-recorded in recovery → add a yes/no field to the recovery chart.
pearls: Recruit the recovery sister to record PONV and rescue.
Present day-case unplanned admissions due to PONV if available.
Pharmacy can confirm drug stock in each anaesthetic room.
Run cycle 1 on the same lists you will re-audit.
effort: ~10 min per 10 cases from electronic anaesthetic and recovery charts
group: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults who vomit or feel sick after surgery despite prophylaxis, what proportion receive their first rescue antiemetic from a different drug class to the prophylaxis?
why: Repeating the same drug (usually ondansetron) soon after prophylaxis gives little extra benefit. No library audit has measured PONV rescue choice.

standard.source: Fifth Consensus Guidelines for the Management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting: Executive Summary (Gan et al., Anesth Analg 2026;143:497–513), Guideline 4
standard.wording: Patients should receive rescue treatment from a different pharmacological class to the prophylactic agents administered. If more than 6 hours has elapsed, administration of a second dose of a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist or butyrophenone may be considered if no alternatives are available.

pass: First rescue antiemetic (in recovery or within 24 hours on the ward) is from a class not used for prophylaxis, or a repeat 5-HT3 antagonist given more than 6 hours after the prophylactic dose.
population: Adults (18+) who received antiemetic prophylaxis during anaesthesia and then received a rescue antiemetic within 24 hours. Exclude patients in ICU.
sample: 40 consecutive patients who received rescue antiemetics, from EPMA/recovery records over 3–4 weeks.
data_source: Anaesthetic chart (prophylactic drugs and times); recovery chart and EPMA (rescue drug and time).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace the generic 'ondansetron PRN' recovery and ward order set with a PONV rescue ladder that lists the drugs given in theatre and suggests a different class first (e.g. cyclizine, prochlorperazine, droperidol).
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 rescue episodes, same template.
close_loop: Present at anaesthetic governance and recovery nursing meeting. If it works, embed the rescue ladder in the post-operative order set.
evidence: [1341] Queen Elizabeth Birmingham surgery: antiemetic co-prescribing with opioids >75% (education, posters, weekly reminders)
[1421] Italian orthopaedic theatres without PACU: nausea/vomiting among causes of unmet discharge criteria (single cycle)
pitfalls: Recovery nurses only have ondansetron under a PGD → update the PGD or order set before cycle 2.
Prophylaxis not recorded clearly → use the electronic chart as the only source.
Droperidol availability varies → offer two alternatives in the ladder.
Ward and recovery rescue differ → report both settings separately.
pearls: Recruit a recovery nurse and a surgical pharmacist.
Collect second-rescue rates; they show the benefit.
Show the ladder on the recovery drug trolley.
Pair this audit with the prophylaxis audit for one presentation.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from charts and EPMA

question: For tracheal intubations outside theatres (ICU, emergency department and wards), what proportion have waveform capnography confirmation of tube placement documented?
why: Unrecognised oesophageal intubation still kills patients outside theatre. Library airway work covers an ED checklist bundle [3008] and a theatre pre-induction checklist [2944], not documented capnography confirmation in ICU and wards.

standard.source: Project for Universal Management of Airways and international airway societies (including DAS), Preventing unrecognised oesophageal intubation: consensus guideline (Anaesthesia 2022)
standard.wording: Exhaled carbon dioxide monitoring and pulse oximetry should be available and used for all episodes of airway management. ... Sustained exhaled carbon dioxide should be used to confirm alveolar ventilation following passage of a tracheal tube

pass: The intubation record documents a sustained waveform capnography trace (or end-tidal CO2 value after ≥7 breaths) as confirmation of tube placement.
population: All adult tracheal intubations and tube exchanges performed in ICU, ED, wards and cardiac arrest calls. Exclude operating theatres.
sample: 40 consecutive out-of-theatre intubations over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ICU/ED intubation checklist or airway record; ICU notes; cardiac arrest audit forms; monitor data if archived.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'Sustained exhaled CO2 confirmed (waveform): yes/no' line to the out-of-theatre intubation checklist and airway record.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 out-of-theatre intubations, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU/ED airway governance and the resuscitation committee. If it works, add capnography to every emergency airway trolley check.
evidence: [3008] Australian major trauma ED: first-attempt success 88.5% → 94.6% (monthly audit, education, intubation checklist)
[2944] Swiss anaesthesia pre-induction checklist: completion 48.3% → 66.7% over five years (single audit series)
pitfalls: Capnography used but not written down → the checklist line fixes documentation; say so when presenting.
Cardiac arrest forms lack the field → update the resuscitation record too.
Low trace in cardiac arrest confuses staff → include the PUMA 'sustained CO2' criteria on the checklist.
Small numbers per month → collect from ICU, ED and arrest calls together.
pearls: Recruit an ICU airway lead and an ED consultant.
Check every emergency airway trolley has a working capnography line during weeks 5–12.
Record videolaryngoscope use at the same time.
Report any recognised oesophageal intubations anonymously.
effort: ~15 min per 10 intubations from airway records
group: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: After thyroid surgery, what proportion of adults have observations including wound inspection recorded at least hourly for the first 6 hours?
why: Neck haematoma after thyroidectomy can obstruct the airway within hours; half occur in the first 6 hours. Library thyroid audits cover calcium and voice outcomes [2487] [2775], not early postoperative monitoring.

standard.source: DAS, BAETS and ENT UK, Management of haematoma after thyroid surgery: consensus guidelines (Anaesthesia 2022)
standard.wording: Thus, routine patient observations should be carried out at least hourly for first 6 h postoperatively ... Minimum monitoring includes wound inspection, early warning and pain scoring, as well as awareness for more subtle signs (agitation; anxiety; difficulty in breathing; discomfort).

pass: Observations (NEWS2, pain score and wound/neck check) recorded with no gap over 60 minutes from recovery discharge until 6 hours after end of surgery.
population: Adults having hemi, total or completion thyroidectomy (and parathyroidectomy via neck incision if agreed). Exclude patients kept in ICU/HDU.
sample: All thyroid operations over the last 6 months (expect 30–50 in a DGH with a thyroid surgeon).
data_source: E-observations or paper charts (times, NEWS2, pain score); nursing notes (wound check); theatre system (end of surgery).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'post-thyroid surgery' observation schedule to the e-observations system (hourly for 6 hours with a neck/wound check field and DESATS prompts), triggered by the procedure code.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14 onward: next 20–30 thyroid operations (low volume), same template.
close_loop: Present at ENT/endocrine surgery and anaesthetic governance. If it works, keep the schedule and add the emergency box check to the ward safety huddle.
evidence: [2487] Somerset thyroidectomy calcium management: guideline followed 100% and no readmissions after a pre-operative pack and updated guidelines
[1221] James Cook spinal surgery: 12/25 → 21/25 post-operative care domains at 100% (post-operative checklist)
pitfalls: Low volume → use 6–12 months for cycle 1 and keep collecting until 20 cases for cycle 2.
Obs recorded but no wound check → the field must be separate.
Patients moved to wards far from the nursing station → record bed location too.
Night staffing pushback → hourly obs apply only to the first 6 hours.
pearls: Recruit the ENT or endocrine ward sister.
Check for the post-thyroid emergency box at the same time.
Invite the thyroid surgeon to co-present.
Use the DAS/BAETS/ENT UK post-thyroid surgery review chart as the template.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from e-observations

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: What proportion of adults with a BMI over 40 are flagged as such on the published theatre list?
why: Airway complications are more frequent in people living with obesity and preparation depends on the team knowing in advance. Library bariatric audits cover cancellations [2724], not theatre-list flags.

standard.source: Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia, Airway management in patients living with obesity: best practice recommendations (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: Operating theatre lists should flag patients with a BMI > 40 kg.m-2 (Grade D, strong recommendation).

pass: The final published theatre list shows BMI or an obesity flag for the patient.
population: Adults with BMI >40 kg/m2 (from pre-assessment or admission weight) on elective or emergency theatre lists, any specialty.
sample: 40 consecutive patients with BMI >40 over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Theatre management system (published list); pre-assessment or admission record (height, weight, BMI); team brief record.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Make BMI a mandatory field when booking a case in the theatre system and display it automatically on the printed and electronic list, with a flag above 40.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 patients with BMI >40, same template.
close_loop: Present at theatre users' group. If it works, add BMI to the WHO team brief script.
evidence: [2724] Chelsea and Westminster bariatric surgery: cancellations 30.5% → 17.3% (early anaesthetic-led pre-assessment)
[3024] NHS theatres WHO checklist: team brief done in 7/8 sessions, debrief 2/8 (single cycle)
pitfalls: BMI missing for emergency cases → allow 'estimated' and record weight on admission.
Patients object to BMI on public screens → show a neutral flag icon rather than the number.
Booking clerks bypass mandatory fields → ask IT to block list publication without BMI.
Definitions change (BMI >35 vs >40) → keep 40 in both cycles.
pearls: Recruit the theatre scheduling manager.
Check emergency lists separately; they fail most.
Show a near miss (equipment not ready) to explain why.
Record team brief discussion as a second measure.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from theatre system

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: For central venous catheters inserted in theatre or intensive care, what proportion have witnessed documentation that the guidewire was removed?
why: A retained guidewire is a Never Event. Library central line audits cover timely removal [2097] and coagulation checks [2399], not guidewire documentation.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: safe vascular access 2025 (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: All possible procedures should be put in place to prevent retained guidewires, including operator vigilance; guidewire counts; mandatory witnessed documentation of guidewire removal; and where available, the use of guidewire anti-retention devices.

pass: The CVC insertion record or LocSSIP checklist states the guidewire was removed and names or signs a second person as witness.
population: All non-tunnelled central venous catheters, dialysis lines and PICCs inserted by anaesthetists or intensivists in theatre, ICU or ED. Exclude tunnelled lines placed in radiology.
sample: 40 consecutive insertions over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: CVC insertion record or LocSSIP sticker in EPR; ICU line log; anaesthetic chart.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace free-text line notes with a vascular access LocSSIP sticker/EPR form that has a 'Guidewire removed and shown to: ___ (signature)' box.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 insertions, same template.
close_loop: Present at ICU and anaesthetic governance and the NatSSIPs group. If it works, make the form the only way to document a line.
evidence: [2097] Surgical ICU central lines: removal alerts created 25% → 65% (step-by-step guide to the electronic alert)
[220] UHBW Stop Before You Block: 80% checked before block → full assurance at re-audit [505] (awareness work)
[508] Stockport prone ventilation safety checklist: significant assurance (single cycle)
pitfalls: Theatre lines documented on the anaesthetic chart only → accept the chart if the witness is named.
Assistants not trained to witness → brief ODPs and ICU nurses before the change.
Paper stickers run out → keep stock in every line trolley and add an EPR version.
Emergency lines out of hours are missed → audit day and night separately.
pearls: Recruit the ICU nurse educator and the theatre ODP lead.
Record ultrasound use too; it is in the same guideline.
Keep a blank form on the CVC trolley.
Present any Never Event learning nationally to show relevance.
effort: ~10 min per 10 insertions from line records
group: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults having major elective surgery with blood cross-matched or a transfusion anticipated, what proportion have a documented pre-operative discussion about transfusion and its alternatives?
why: Valid consent for transfusion is a national requirement, yet documentation is patchy; a general surgery audit improved it after feedback [2434]. No audit has targeted major elective surgery before the day of operation.

standard.source: Association of Anaesthetists guidelines: the use of blood components and their alternatives (Anaesthesia 2025), recommendation 2
standard.wording: Where blood transfusion is anticipated, this and alternatives to transfusion should be discussed with the patient before surgery, and their consent should be documented according to local protocols.

pass: Consent form, pre-assessment or anaesthetic note documents a discussion of transfusion risks, benefits and alternatives, and the patient's decision, before the day of surgery or before induction.
population: Adults having major elective non-orthopaedic surgery (e.g. colorectal, hepatobiliary, upper GI, gynae-oncology, urology, vascular) for whom blood was cross-matched or a transfusion was judged likely.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Blood bank cross-match list; surgical consent form; pre-assessment and anaesthetic pre-op notes; transfusion record.

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a transfusion section (risks, benefits, alternatives, leaflet given, decision) to the consent form or anaesthetic pre-op template for procedures with a cross-match on the maximum surgical blood ordering schedule.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the hospital transfusion committee and surgical governance. If it works, include the section in all major surgery consent forms.
evidence: [2434] District general surgery inpatients: most transfusion documentation criteria above 80% after discussion with junior doctors
[2515] East Sussex general surgery: NICE-compliant units 40.2% → 50.4% (teaching, posters)
pitfalls: Surgeons and anaesthetists each assume the other consents → agree who owns it before cycle 1.
Consent recorded only when transfusion happens → sample from the cross-match list, not the transfusion list.
Jehovah's Witness patients distort results → include them; an advance decision counts as a documented discussion.
Section left blank on the form → make it mandatory for listed procedures.
pearls: Recruit the transfusion practitioner.
Use the NHS Blood and Transplant patient leaflet.
Link the change to the maximum surgical blood ordering schedule.
Report alternatives offered; it supports patient blood management.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from consent forms and notes

area: Anaesthesia, perioperative care and intensive care
question: In adults using CPAP or home non-invasive ventilation who have elective surgery, what proportion are told at pre-assessment to bring their machine on the day of surgery?
why: Patients with obstructive sleep apnoea who arrive without their CPAP face higher postoperative respiratory risk and may need HDU beds. No library audit covers this.

standard.source: Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia, Airway management in patients living with obesity: best practice recommendations (Anaesthesia 2025)
standard.wording: Patients on CPAP/non-invasive ventilation should be instructed to bring their machine on the day of surgery (Grade C, strong recommendation).

pass: Pre-assessment record or letter documents the instruction to bring the machine, and the admission record shows it arrived.
population: Adults using CPAP, APAP or home NIV for any indication having elective surgery with an anaesthetist.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over 4–6 weeks.
data_source: Pre-assessment record and patient letters; admission checklist; recovery/ward notes (CPAP used post-op).

template.note: Local audit code only; no names or NHS numbers

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add 'Uses CPAP/NIV: bring machine and mask on day of surgery' as an automatic line in the pre-assessment admission letter when CPAP is ticked.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at the pre-assessment team and anaesthetic governance. If it works, add a 'CPAP on ward' check to the recovery discharge criteria.
evidence: [2724] Chelsea and Westminster bariatric surgery: cancellations 30.5% → 17.3% (early anaesthetic-led pre-assessment)
[2944] Swiss pre-induction checklist: completion 48.3% → 66.7% over five years (single audit series)
pitfalls: CPAP use not asked at pre-assessment → add a yes/no question first.
Patients forget despite instruction → add a text reminder the day before.
Wards lack power points or staff familiar with CPAP → involve the respiratory nurse.
Small numbers → extend the collection window.
pearls: Recruit the sleep or respiratory physiology team.
Include day-surgery units.
Record post-op CPAP use as an outcome.
Keep the same inclusion in both cycles.
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from pre-assessment and admission records

question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more with suspected infection) receive IV antibiotics within 1 hour of their first ED NEWS2 score?
why: NG253 (2025, updated 2026) fixes time zero as the first ED NEWS2 score. Library sepsis audits used older bundles and screening tools [3007][2618]; none measures the 1-hour limit from the NEWS2 time stamp.

standard.wording: Give people aged 16 or over who are at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic treatment, within 1 hour of calculating the person's NEWS2 score on initial assessment in the emergency department or on ward deterioration. Only give antibiotics if they have not been given before for this episode of sepsis (see recommendations 1.7.7 and 1.7.8 on managing the condition while awaiting transfer).

pass: First IV antibiotic dose recorded as given on the drug chart within 60 minutes of the first ED NEWS2 time; or pre-hospital antibiotics already given for this episode.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected or confirmed infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 7 or more. Exclude end-of-life care plans and patients who left before treatment.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible ED attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED system or e-observations for first NEWS2 time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic administration time; ambulance record for pre-hospital antibiotics.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic ED alert on the e-observations system: a NEWS2 of 7 or more with an 'infection suspected' tick opens a sepsis order set with a pre-filled antibiotic and a 60-minute countdown on the tracking board.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 consecutive eligible attendances, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED governance and the Trust deteriorating patient group. If it works, keep the alert in the e-observations build and report monthly to the sepsis lead.
evidence: [3007] paediatric severe sepsis: antibiotics within 1 hour 42% at baseline (no standard met)
[1847] delirium: compulsory electronic screen raised completion 3% → 87% (system change beats teaching)
[1358] ED VTE assessment: electronic discharge prompt 32% → 93.1% (electronic prompt)
pitfalls: Time zero recorded differently between cycles → agree in advance that time zero is the first ED NEWS2 time stamp, not triage or doctor review.
Prescription time used instead of administration time → take only the 'given' time from EPMA.
Medium-risk patients with a 3-point single parameter caused by infection are missed → add a column and decide inclusion rules before cycle 1.
Nursing staff see the audit as blame → share results by shift pattern, not by name.
Gains fade after rotation → make the alert part of the system, not a poster.
pearls: Recruit the ED sepsis nurse and the EPR analyst on day 1; they can pull NEWS2 time stamps in bulk.
Record the reason for each delay; the commonest cause tells you which fix to pick.
Use a run chart of weekly compliance, not a single percentage.
Hand the monthly report to a consultant owner before you rotate.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from e-observations and EPMA

question: What proportion of adults at high risk from sepsis who receive IV fluid in the ED are given an initial bolus of 250 ml?
why: NG253 (2025) cut the first sepsis bolus from 500 ml to 250 ml with reassessment after each bolus. Old habits and pre-printed sepsis stickers still say 500 ml. No audit of bolus volume is published in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.6 and 1.8.8 (November 2025, updated September 2026)
standard.wording: 1.8.6 Give an initial bolus of 250 ml. Ideally, give this over 10 to 15 minutes. [2025] ... 1.8.8 Reassess after each fluid bolus. [2025]

pass: First resuscitation bolus prescribed and given as 250 ml of crystalloid, with a documented reassessment (observations or clinical note) before any further bolus.
population: Adults 16 or over at high risk from sepsis (NEWS2 7 or more, or medium risk with hypoperfusion) given IV fluid resuscitation in the ED. Exclude patients in cardiac arrest.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: EPMA or fluid chart for volume and time; e-observations and clinical notes for reassessment.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive
Pass criterion 2; 'not applicable' if one bolus only

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Replace the sepsis order set default from '500 ml bolus' to '250 ml over 10–15 minutes, reassess' and reprint the sepsis sticker with the same wording.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients, same template.
close_loop: Present at ED and acute medicine governance. If it works, lock the new default into the order set and add it to the ED induction pack.
evidence: [1517] arthroplasty analgesia: electronic order set raised full protocol compliance 0/27 → 58% (order set default)
[2471] ED renal colic: renal order set lifted NSAID use 54.5% → 71.9% (order set)
[2196] emergency surgery VTE doses: two checkboxes added to the drug chart, correct dosing 29/36 → 37/38 (chart redesign)
pitfalls: Old 500 ml bags or stickers left in resus → remove old stock labels and stickers on the change date.
Paramedic pre-alert fluids counted as the first bolus → record pre-hospital fluid separately.
Clinicians object that 250 ml is too little in shock → share the NG253 wording and stress repeat boluses up to 1,000 ml.
Reassessment not written down → accept a timed set of observations as reassessment.
pearls: Agree definitions with the ED sepsis lead before cycle 1.
Ask pharmacy to change the order set default; it is quick and lasts beyond rotation.
Pair the audit with the antibiotic timing audit to share data collection.
Report total fluid in the first hour too, to show no one is under-resuscitated.
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from EPMA and fluid chart

question: What proportion of adults at medium risk from sepsis (NEWS2 5 or 6 with suspected infection) are reviewed by an FY2-level or more senior clinician, with the venous lactate result, within 1 hour?
why: NG253 (2024, amended 2026) allows antibiotics to be deferred up to 3 hours for medium-risk patients only if a competent clinician reviews them and the lactate within 1 hour. No library audit covers the medium-risk group.

standard.wording: For people aged 16 or over with a medium risk of severe illness or death from sepsis: carry out a venous blood test, including for: blood gas, including glucose and lactate measurement ... arrange for a clinician with core competencies in the care of acutely ill patients (FY2 level or above) to review the person's condition and venous lactate results within 1 hour of the person being assessed as at medium risk. [2024, amended 2026]

pass: A timed clinical note by an FY2 or more senior clinician, mentioning the lactate result, within 60 minutes of the first NEWS2 of 5 or 6.
population: Adults 16 or over with suspected infection and a first ED NEWS2 of 5 or 6. Exclude patients who became high risk before review.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible attendances over the last 2 months.
data_source: E-observations for NEWS2 time; blood gas analyser or lab system for lactate time; ED notes for reviewer grade and time.

template.note: Local audit code only; key kept on a Trust drive

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a 'medium sepsis risk' flag to the ED tracking board that starts a 60-minute timer and prompts an automatic venous gas at triage.
reaudit: Weeks 13–14: next 40 eligible patients.
close_loop: Present at ED governance. If it works, keep the flag and include medium-risk review in the monthly sepsis dashboard.
evidence: [3007] paediatric sepsis: lactate done 89% but timed care standards all missed (timing is the gap)
[2174] ED frailty: mandatory field in ED software raised CFS recording 40% → 100% (system change)
[1781] delirium: stickers and emails peaked then fell to 1.3% by week 6 (paper prompts fade)
pitfalls: Grade of reviewer not recorded → use the rota or login name to confirm grade.
Lactate done on the arterial gas instead → accept any blood gas lactate.
Patients escalate to high risk and drop out → record them and analyse separately.
Night-time staffing skews results → report by time of day.
pearls: Get the ED nurse in charge to agree triage-led venous gas before cycle 1.
Pull NEWS2 5–6 plus infection codes from the EPR to find cases fast.
Record the antibiotic decision to show safe deferral, not just speed.
Present results with the high-risk antibiotic audit as one sepsis story.
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients

question: What proportion of children under 16 with suspected sepsis who meet a NICE high risk criterion receive antibiotics within 1 hour of meeting that criterion in the ED?
why: NG254 (2025) keeps the 1-hour antibiotic limit for high-risk children. The library shows antibiotics within 1 hour in only 42% [3007] and a local paperwork redesign without published figures [279].

standard.wording: Ensure urgent assessment mechanisms are in place to deliver antibiotics when any high risk criteria are met in a person under 16 in secondary care (within 1 hour of meeting a high risk criterion in an acute hospital setting). [2016]

pass: First antibiotic dose given (IV or IO) within 60 minutes of the first recorded high risk criterion.
population: Children under 16 attending the ED with suspected sepsis and at least one NG254 high risk criterion. Exclude those given antibiotics before arrival.
sample: 30–40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3–6 months.
data_source: Paediatric ED notes and PEWS charts for criterion time; EPMA or drug chart for antibiotic time.

question: What proportion of adults with a head injury and a NICE 1-hour CT risk factor have their CT head scan within 1 hour of that risk factor being identified?
why: NG232 (2023) sets a 1-hour limit for high-risk adults. The library head injury work measured neurosurgical advice time [2101] and c-spine imaging in older adults [1147]; none measures the 1-hour CT limit.

standard.wording: For people 16 and over who have sustained a head injury, do a CT head scan within 1 hour of any of these risk factors being identified: a GCS score of 12 or less on initial assessment in the emergency department; a GCS score of less than 15 at 2 hours after the injury on assessment in the emergency department; suspected open or depressed skull fracture; any sign of basal skull fracture (haemotympanum, 'panda' eyes, cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the ear or nose, Battle's sign); post-traumatic seizure; focal neurological deficit; more than 1 episode of vomiting. [2023]

pass: CT acquisition time within 60 minutes of the first documented risk factor time.
population: Adults 16 or over with head injury and at least one rec 1.5.8 risk factor. Exclude patients already scanned elsewhere.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2–3 months.
data_source: ED notes for risk factor and time; PACS/RIS for request and scan times.

question: What proportion of adults on anticoagulants with a head injury and no other CT indication have a documented CT decision with a reason?
why: NG232 (2023) changed anticoagulated head injury from 'scan all' to 'consider CT within 8 hours'. Many EDs still scan by habit or discharge without a recorded decision. No audit of this change is published in the library.

standard.wording: For people who have sustained a head injury and have no other indications for a CT head scan, but are on anticoagulant treatment (including vitamin K antagonists, direct-acting oral anticoagulants (DOACs), heparin and low molecular weight heparins) or antiplatelet treatment (excluding aspirin monotherapy), consider doing a CT head scan: within 8 hours of the injury (for example, if it is difficult to do a risk assessment or if the person might not return to the emergency department if they have signs of deterioration) or within the hour if they present more than 8 hours after the injury.

pass: Notes record a CT decision (scan or no scan) and a reason; if scanned, CT within 8 hours of injury (or within 1 hour if presenting after 8 hours).
population: Adults 16 or over on anticoagulant or non-aspirin antiplatelet therapy with head injury and no rec 1.5.8 or 1.5.9 risk factors.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible patients over the last 2 months.
data_source: ED notes and medication history; RIS for CT times.

question: What proportion of children with a head injury and exactly one NICE risk factor are observed for at least 4 hours from the time of injury?
why: NG232 (2023) asks for 4 hours of observation when a child has only one rec 1.5.11 risk factor. Early discharge is common in busy EDs. No library audit covers paediatric head injury observation.

If none of these risk factors occur during observation, use clinical judgement to determine whether a longer period of observation is needed. [2023]

pass: Documented observations continue until at least 4 hours after the time of injury before discharge.
population: Children under 16 with head injury and exactly one rec 1.5.11 risk factor and no rec 1.5.10 factor.
sample: 40 consecutive eligible children over the last 3 months.
data_source: Paediatric head injury proforma, PEWS and neuro-observation chart, ED discharge time.

sample: 50 consecutive discharges over 2–4 weeks.

question: What proportion of adults discharged from the ED with atrial fibrillation have a CHA2DS2-VASc score documented?

question: What proportion of adults with cirrhosis and ascites on long-term antibiotic prophylaxis for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis meet a NICE indication for it?

population: Adults admitted with an acute exacerbation of COPD who were prescribed nebulised bronchodilators. Exclude patients on invasive ventilation.

question: What proportion of adults treated for community-acquired pneumonia have antibiotics stopped at 5 days, or a documented reason to continue?
why: Five-day courses are the NICE default, reaffirmed in the 2025 pneumonia guideline. Library stewardship audits focused on surgical courses [2756, 2844] and review dates [2465]; no medical CAP duration audit is in the library.

standard.wording: For adults with community-acquired pneumonia, stop antibiotic treatment after 5 days unless: microbiological results suggest a longer course is needed or the person is not clinically stable, for example, if they have had a fever in the past 48 hours or have more than 1 of the following signs of clinical instability: systolic blood pressure less than 90 mmHg; heart rate more than 100 beats per minute; respiratory rate more than 24 breaths per minute; oxygen saturations of less than 90% on room air (or failure to meet long-term baseline oxygen requirements) [2019, amended 2025]

pass: Total antibiotic course (IV plus oral, inpatient plus discharge) is 5 days, or a longer course has a documented reason matching the NICE exceptions.
population: Adults admitted with community-acquired pneumonia and treated with antibiotics. Exclude aspiration pneumonia, empyema, lung abscess, Legionella, Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, immunosuppression and deaths before day 5.
sample: 40 consecutive CAP discharges over the last 6 weeks.
data_source: Coding for cases; e-prescribing for start and stop dates; discharge prescription; observations chart for day 5 stability; microbiology results.

question: What proportion of adult inpatients with confirmed C. difficile infection have their proton pump inhibitor reviewed within 48 hours of the result?
